overview: Bolivia declared independence in 1825, before this map interval. The modern state encompasses many Indigenous and other communities whose schools, crafts, healing knowledge and political struggles cannot be reduced to a single culture.

periods.title: Independent republic
periods.summary: Independence in 1825 preceded the map’s 1878 start and later struggles over participation.

periods.title: Revolution and contested government
periods.summary: Reforms extended voting and nationalized major mines; later military governments interrupted civilian rule.

periods.title: Civilian government and plurinational recognition
periods.summary: Civilian government returned in 1982; the 2009 constitution describes a plurinational state.

items.text: The Casa de la Libertad commemorates the deputies who signed the independence act on 6 August 1825. Its portraits include Casimiro Olañeta painted by Melchor María Mercado. Portraits preserve how political figures were represented, alongside the documentary record of their actions.

The 1952 revolution expanded suffrage to women and adults excluded by literacy requirements. This changed who could participate in national elections. Independence had not automatically brought equal political participation a century earlier.

Nationalization in 1952 transferred major tin-mining enterprises to state control. Agricultural reform followed in 1953. These measures changed ownership and rural relationships; they were political and economic transformations rather than the disappearance of Bolivian communities.

Avelino Siñani and Elizardo Pérez founded the Warisata school in 1931. Its school-ayllu model drew on community organization and collective work. Education here was an Indigenous-led effort to connect learning with the practical needs of local life.

Warisata included workshops whose production helped sustain the school, alongside a community parliament and student responsibilities. The model treated making, governing and learning as connected activities. A lesson could involve useful work beyond a desk.

Kallawaya healers learn through apprenticeship and travel across different environments, building knowledge of plants and ritual practice. UNESCO records this specialized Andean tradition. Describing its cultural knowledge does not establish that every historical remedy was effective.

The Kallawaya account also identifies women’s work in maternal and child care and in weaving textiles used in ritual settings. Healing knowledge belongs within a wider social world of relationships, images and ceremonies, rather than an isolated collection of ingredients.

In 2017, eight Kallawaya communities helped produce a publication documenting their knowledge. Distribution was intended for the communities themselves to support younger generations. Preservation did not require turning every piece of knowledge into a public commodity.

During Alasita in La Paz, people acquire miniature objects associated with hopes and wishes. They may seek Andean ritual consecration or Catholic blessings. The tiny objects express what participants value; the account records belief, not a promise that miniatures can fulfill wishes.

People also exchange Alasita miniatures as symbolic payments of debts. This creates a social meaning beyond buying a souvenir. A very small object can stand for a much larger relationship between people.

Children commonly learn Alasita practices while accompanying parents, and craft competitions encourage makers’ creativity. The tradition connects family learning with skilled miniature production. Its 2017 UNESCO recognition concerns living practice, not an abandoned ancient ritual.

Article 8 of Bolivia’s 2009 constitution includes the Quechua words “ama qhilla, ama llulla, ama suwa”: “do not be lazy, do not lie, do not steal.” This is the spelling printed in that legal witness. A modern constitutional quotation is not an ancient manuscript or a statement that everyone speaks Quechua.

ending.text: Bolivia continues as a state. Civilian government returned in 1982, and the 2009 constitutional framework recognized its plurinational character. Political institutions changed while its many peoples continued. The map’s 1878 starting point does not date their origins or the 1825 republic.
